Juveniles of the Blunt-nosed leopard lizard (Gambelia sila) emerge from their leathery-shelled eggs after an incubation period of approximately 61 days [ab = approximately 61 days] when maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. At the moment of hatching, these neonates possess a snout-vent length (SVL) of about 4.5 cm [Lb = about 4.5 cm], reflecting the modest size of the egg from which they emerge. The wet weight of these newly emerged young is typically around 3.3 g [Wwb = around 3.3 g], a measurement that aligns with the calculated mass derived from the egg dimensions. This initial size places them among the smallest of the crotaphytid lizards, necessitating a rapid growth phase to reduce vulnerability to a wide array of predators, including snakes, raptors, and larger mammalian carnivores that share their arid grassland and scrub habitats in the San Joaquin Valley of California.

As these immature individuals progress through the juvenile stage, their growth trajectory is heavily influenced by seasonal prey abundance. Field studies tracking recaptured animals indicate that females typically achieve sexual maturation upon reaching a snout-vent length of approximately 8.8 cm [Lp = approximately 8.8 cm]. Males of this species require a slightly larger body size to trigger the onset of gonadal activity, with puberty generally attained at an SVL of around 9.8 cm [Lp = around 9.8 cm], as estimated from growth curve data at the time of puberty. This difference in size at maturation is a common pattern among sexually dimorphic reptiles, often linked to the differing energetic demands of egg production versus male-male competition for territory and mates. Upon reaching maturity, these reproductively viable adults continue to grow, albeit at a decelerating rate, approaching their final body dimensions. The period of juvenile growth is critical for accumulating the energy reserves needed to survive the first hibernation, and mortality during this stage can be substantial when prey resources are scarce.

The ultimate body size of adult Gambelia sila shows a pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females reaching a smaller asymptotic snout-vent length of 11.2 cm [Li = 11.2 cm], whereas males can attain an ultimate SVL of 11.9 cm [Li = 11.9 cm]. This disparity is mirrored in their wet body masses; gravid females reach a maximum adult wet weight of about 16.8 g [Wwi = about 16.8 g], while males, with their more robust frames and larger heads used in aggressive displays, can achieve an ultimate wet weight of approximately 20.2 g [Wwi = approximately 20.2 g]. These values are derived from size-corrected allometric relationships observed in related lacertid lizards, suggesting a conserved scaling pattern within the clade. The larger male body size is likely an adaptation facilitating success in intraspecific combat during the breeding season, although it also increases their relative metabolic demands and may constrain male survival under resource-limited conditions.

Under the warm thermal conditions characteristic of their active season, typically 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time from birth until the attainment of sexual maturity is approximately 9 months. More precisely, the time since birth at puberty is around 274.5 d [tp = around 274.5 d], a period that encompasses their first full overwintering hibernation. at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]For males, this same milestone occurs at a similar chronological age, though it is reached at a slightly larger body size due to their faster growth rate. Upon reaching adulthood, the maximum recorded longevity for this species under similar environmental conditions is roughly 5 years [am = roughly 5 years] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan is relatively short compared to other large-bodied phrynosomatids, reflecting the high metabolic costs associated with their active foraging strategy and unpredictable prey base within their highly seasonal, semi-arid environment. Mortality spikes are often observed during droughts when insect populations crash, highlighting the tight coupling between their life history and climatic variability.

Female reproductive output is constrained by both clutch size and the number of nesting events per season. Field surveys from the Carrizo Plain indicate that a single clutch contains, on average, 2.4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2.4 eggs per clutch], and a typical female produces about 1.2 such clutches within a single active season [F_R_i = about 1.2 such clutches within a single active season]. This results in an annual reproductive output that is remarkably low for a lizard of its body size, which translates to an approximate maximum daily reproduction rate of 0.0079 eggs per day [Ri = 0.0079 eggs per day], a life-history strategy that may be linked to the extreme physiological challenges of the environment. The timing of this first egg clutch, or age at first reproduction, is tightly tied to the attainment of the necessary body mass; consequently, these events occur after the female has reached her pubertal size, ensuring she has sufficient energy reserves for vitellogenesis and successful embryonic development within the parchment-shelled eggs.
